note:
Hand-written letters with asserted rubric scores, for `npm run outreach -- --rubric-fixtures`. This is the drill that makes the drafting loop a quality bar rather than a vibe, and the argument is in rubric.ts's header: a model judge returns a different number for the same letter next week, so there is nothing to assert against, and this module can be asserted against. The profile and the posting are supplied here rather than read from data/profile.md, for the same reason policy.json supplies its own preferences — a drill whose expected values move when unrelated content is edited is a drill people learn to ignore.

Two of the cases are *good* letters, in deliberately different registers, and they matter more than the eleven bad ones: a rubric that only ever proves it can reject has not been checked for false positives, and a false positive here is the loop throwing away the letter Davit would actually have sent. The first run of this drill failed both of them, on "Keeping those figures true" and "Thank you in advance" being read as invented employers.

Note what the blocked cases do *not* assert: a low total. A letter reading "Dear [Hiring Manager]" still scores in the high eighties, because its prose is good and the total is about the prose. "You cannot send this" is what `blockers` is for, and `rankings` below asserts the consequence that matters — a clean letter outranks a blocked one however well the blocked one is written.

The `money` category is §5 made deterministic. A prompt instruction saying "do not mention salary" cannot be asserted against; this can. Its false-positive case has its own fixture and is the one that matters, because this profile is full of numbers that are the whole point of it — 100,000 requests per minute, p95 under 500 ms, Java 17. A bare number never matches; a number wearing a currency does.

EVERY FIGURE IN THE MONEY CASE IS INVENTED, and it is written as a *fictional employer's published band* rather than as anything the candidate asks for. That is deliberate and it is a §5 matter, not a style one: this file is committed, git history cannot be edited afterwards, and a realistic-looking salary sitting next to Davit's name in a letter written in his first person reads as his real number whatever a comment says. His actual figures live in private/job-preferences.md, which is gitignored, and nothing here is derived from them. A posting's published band is also the more honest test: it is the shape the money rule actually guards against, since stage B's prompt receives `compensation` and can echo it into `verdict.reasons`.

Davit Hayrapetyan is a software architect based in Yerevan, Armenia, with
fourteen years on JVM platforms.

## Raymond James
Led the modernization of a wealth-management platform on Java 17 and Spring Boot.
The platform sustains peaks of around 100,000 requests per minute; p50 latency is
around 80 ms and p95 is held under 500 ms.

## jambit GmbH
Built a driver-licence platform for a German public-sector client, on Java and
PostgreSQL, as the engineer other people brought designs to.

## Grid Dynamics
Distributed services and Kafka-based event pipelines for retail clients, including
the migration of a monolith to event-driven services.

## Talkdesk
Contact-centre platform work on AWS.

## Novanoweb
Earlier full-stack work on Java and Angular.

Tools: Java, Spring Boot, Kafka, PostgreSQL, AWS, Docker, Git.

cases.name: a good letter: checkable numbers, this posting's requirements, no markers
cases.body:
Hi — I'm Davit Hayrapetyan, a software architect in Yerevan, and I'm writing about the Staff Backend Engineer role at Aurelia Systems.

The part of the posting I'd point at first is the high-throughput ingestion pipeline. At Raymond James I led the modernization of a wealth-management platform on Java 17 and Spring Boot that sustains peaks of around 100,000 requests per minute, with p50 latency around 80 ms and p95 held under 500 ms. Those numbers were the thing we defended release by release, and defending them is most of what owning a pipeline's reliability turns out to mean.

The migration from a monolith to event-driven services is the other half of it. At Grid Dynamics I worked on distributed services and Kafka-based event pipelines for retail clients, which is the same shape of problem: deciding what becomes an event, what stays a call, and what the system does when a consumer falls behind.

I've also spent several years as the senior engineer other people bring designs to, at jambit and at Talkdesk. If the pipeline work is the priority, that is where I would start.

cases.name: a second good letter in a plainer register scores as well as the first
cases.body:
Hello — my name is Davit Hayrapetyan. I am a software architect in Yerevan and I am writing about the Staff Backend Engineer role at Aurelia Systems.

At Raymond James I led the modernization of a wealth-management platform built on Java 17 and Spring Boot. It sustains peaks of around 100,000 requests per minute, p50 latency sits around 80 ms, and p95 is held under 500 ms. Keeping those figures true under load is the closest thing I have to a specialism, and it is what your posting describes as owning the reliability of a payments ingestion pipeline.

Before that, at Grid Dynamics, I worked on Kafka-based event pipelines and on the migration of a monolith to event-driven services. At jambit I built a driver-licence platform for a German public-sector client on Java and PostgreSQL, and was the senior engineer the team brought its designs to.

That is the work I want to keep doing. My CV and a fuller account of each of those platforms are a click away if it is useful.
